newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia feels heat of oil price but impact moderate.
newsitem.headline: Asia feels heat of oil price but impact moderate.

text.p: Asia's oil importers are fretting over increasing crude oil prices as they begin to feel the sting of rising import bills.
They are worrying about their balances of payments and are concerned about higher inflation as increasing prices are passed on to the customer, analysts said on Thursday.
"Compared with 1995, crude prices this year are nine to 10 percent higher," said former OPEC secretary general Subroto.
"The higher prices will certainly put pressure on the balance of trade and balance of payments of consuming countries," Subroto, who now heads a private energy think-tank in Indonesia, told Reuters.

Vishvanath Desai, the Asian Development Bank's energy industry director, said the impact of oil prices was declining thanks to improved energy efficiency, conservation and the use of alternative fuels.

"In the early 1980s, when oil prices were very high, countries here paid 30-40 percent of their export earnings to import oil," Desai said. "But today, nobody has to pay more than 15-20 percent at the most."

Benchmark Brent crude prices jumped in early September with the explosion of tension between the United States and Iraq to a post Gulf War high of $24.39 a barrel. At the end of August, it was $18.63 a barrel. Now, as tensions ease, it is $22.15.
Subroto said he expected prices to remain high until the end of the year because a United Nations/Iraq oil deal has been put on hold because of Iraq's incursion into northern Kurdish areas.

Baghdad had been due to sell oil worth $2.0 billion over six months to pay for food and medicines as an exemption to an embargo resulting from the 1991 Gulf War. Such sales would have pushed crude prices down.
How long oil prices will stay high is of special interest to Japan. Official figures show its August crude import bill rose 53.8 percent from a year earlier, mainly due to higher prices.

Crude oil made up 8.9 percent of overall imports last year. "It is a big chunk and we are keeping very careful watch over the global crude oil trade and price movements," a Finance Ministry official said.

Economists said the price rise could deepen South Korea's snowballing trade deficit and spiralling inflation. Crude imports account for more than eight percent of its imports -- 12.4 percent when oil products are included.
"South Korea is likely to end up the biggest victim in Asia of strong oil prices," said Shin Hoo-shik, a senior economist at the private Daewoo Economic Research Institute in Seoul.
Higher crude prices will hurt India, too.

India's external trade as a percentage of GDP is a low 22.6 percent and oil accounts for 21 percent of imports. "The base on which you have to finance oil imports is narrow," said Sanjeev Sanyal, an economist at Crosby Ltd.

Ramdeo Agarwal, research head at Motilal Oswal Securities, said Indian industry was still reeling from an oil product price rise in July. "Even to think of another price hike is nerve-shattering," he said. "It will be very bad at a time when the economy itself is slowing down."
China has cut crude imports since the Iraqi crisis pushed up prices, industry sources said. Chinese officials dismissed any real impact of higher prices on its economy.
Economists and government officials were divided over the impact on Thailand. The rise has been "acceptable" and would not harm the economy, said senior official Metta Banturngsuk.
But Lehman Brothers economist Paul Alapat said higher prices would further jeopardise Thailand's trade and current account deficits, both among the highest in the region.

Sri Lanka, wholly dependent on imports, is looking at a higher trade deficit. Analysts said they expected higher prices at the pump when the government, faced with a ballooning budget deficit, presents next year's budget on November 6.
For net crude exporters Indonesia and Malaysia, higher prices are better news.
"Indonesia will receive around $600 million for every dollar increase above the price envisaged in the budget," said Baharuddin, director of state-owned oil company Pertamina.
"However, 47 percent of this will be swallowed by crude purchases to feed our refineries."
High oil prices will boost Indonesia's GDP growth because "the industrial sector that uses raw material from oil-based products will grow too," said senior official Miranda Gultom.
Malaysia could earn around $3.6 billion from oil exports at current prices, up from sales worth an estimated $2.64 billion in 1995, analysts said.
But since oil accounted for only 3.6 percent of exports in 1995, that would only have a marginal impact on GDP, said Rajeev Malek, economist at Jardine Fleming.
